name: Otis Redding
hook: A Macon singer who started out copying Little Richard, got his chance at Stax as a driver for another act, wrote 'Respect', and died in a plane crash before his biggest hit came out.

blurb.age13: Otis Redding was born in Dawson, Georgia, in 1941 and grew up in a public housing project in Macon. His father was a sharecropper. He left school at 15 to support his family, and his first hero was Little Richard, also from Macon, whose old backing band he worked with. In 1962 he drove a guitarist to a recording session at Stax in Memphis; at the end, he was allowed to sing two songs, and the label signed him. Backed by Stax's house band, he became one of soul's greatest singers. He wrote 'Respect', which Aretha Franklin later made her own. In June 1967 he played the Monterey Pop Festival to a mostly white audience for the first time. That December his plane crashed into a lake in Wisconsin and he died, aged 26. '(Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay', recorded days before, became the first record to reach number one after its singer had died.
blurb.adult: Born in Dawson on 9 September 1941, the son of a sharecropper, and raised from age three in Macon's Tindall Heights housing project. He left school at 15 to support the family, worked with Little Richard's former backing band the Upsetters, and modelled himself on Little Richard; he won a local talent show singing Richard's 'Heebie Jeebies'. Sam Cooke was his other main model, especially 'Sam Cooke at the Copa'. In 1962 he drove the guitarist Johnny Jenkins to a Stax session; when it ended early he was allowed two songs, and Jim Stewart, who thought the first sounded too much like Little Richard, signed him on the strength of the ballad 'These Arms of Mine' (Volt, October 1962). With the Stax house band, Booker T. and the M.G.'s at its core, he made 'Otis Blue' (1965), which included his own 'Respect' and a cover of the Rolling Stones' 'Satisfaction'. Monterey Pop in June 1967, booked through Jerry Wexler, was his first major performance to a white American audience. He died when his plane crashed into Lake Monona, near Madison, Wisconsin, on 10 December 1967, aged 26. '(Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay', written with Steve Cropper, became the first posthumous number one on both the Hot 100 and the R&B chart.
